source.title: Train longer, generalize better: closing the generalization gap in large batch training of neural networks
source.authors: Elad Hoffer; Itay Hubara; Daniel Soudry

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including the appendix; no material truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares small- and large-batch training and tests learning-rate, batch-normalization, and training-regime adjustments against the large-batch generalization gap.
record.gate_note: The study reports validation accuracy for small-batch, large-batch, and adjusted large-batch training. The paper also reports weight-distance measurements and a loss-variation experiment relevant to its proposed account; these are included as separate rows. It does not test the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures held-out image-classification accuracy across batch sizes under the original epoch schedules, then tests learning-rate scaling, Ghost Batch Normalization, and longer training. It is an original source for V5, so verdict labels are suppressed.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase accurately represents the authors' conclusion: they attribute the observed gap to insufficient updates and argue that learning-rate scaling, GBN, and sufficiently many high-learning-rate updates can eliminate it. They also report that GBN reduces the gap without additional updates. Qualify this as their interpretation of the tested settings: the interventions are combined, WResNet remains 0.13 percentage points below its small-batch reference, and the study leaves training speedups unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: Momentum SGD with learning-rate schedules; compares small and large batches, then changes learning-rate scaling, Ghost Batch Normalization, and iteration count. Does not test arbitrary-label memorization or the other listed interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size and training-regime adaptation change validation accuracy; learning-rate adjustment and Ghost Batch Normalization reduce but do not consistently eliminate the small/large-batch difference, while regime adaptation closes it in the reported comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight distance from initialization grows approximately logarithmically with update count; learning-rate scaling and GBN make slopes more similar across batch sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-training weight displacement follows approximately logarithmic dynamics, with batch-dependent diffusion rates.

fits_no_version.finding: The standard deviation of loss differences around initialization grows approximately linearly with weight distance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Local loss statistics around initialization are consistent with the proposed random-potential model.

record.problems: Validation accuracy is reported without uncertainty estimates. The main comparison is across batch sizes and training adjustments; no explicit random-label memorization capability check is reported. ImageNet experiments are described as using batch 2048 due to memory limitations, while the table's large-batch notation refers to 4096/8192 settings.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width changes beyond the width required for interpolation.
Controlled comparisons of convolutional and fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Own experimental comparisons of adaptive optimizers with SGD; the discussion cites other work.

Language models; systematic identification of workload-dependent batch thresholds; linear learning-rate scaling with warmup as a successful remedy; recovery within the original epoch budget. The regime-adapted results explicitly increase epochs.
Whether adding dropout lowers held-out error. The statement that dropout did not reduce the batch-size gap does not establish its absolute effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness at trained solutions, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of memorized training examples and retraining.

missing.what: The second AlexNet condition uses batch 8192: +LR+GBN reaches 53.93% versus 57.10% small-batch accuracy, and +RA reaches 59.5%. Record these separately. The repeated LB and +LR entries are batch-2048 measurements under footnote 8, not independent batch-8192 results.
missing.locator: Table 2, second AlexNet row and footnote 8

missing.what: The authors explicitly report that dropout, dropconnect, and label noise did not help reduce the large-batch generalization gap. This qualitative negative result on alternative recipe adjustments is unrecorded; configurations and numerical effects are not supplied.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are assigned because arXiv:1705.08741 is an original source for V5. Observed states on regime-adapted rows refer to V5's recovery qualification; partial states on LR/GBN rows refer to incomplete recovery. Architecture citations in subject names identify model designs, not externally sourced table results. Table 1 values are the study's own experiments. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
Language models; batches beyond workload-dependent sizes as a general rule; equal-epoch comparisons for all adjusted methods; normalization or regularization changes beyond Ghost Batch Normalization.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

relation.reason: Reports its own small- and large-batch generalization comparisons and recovery experiments.

tranche.reason: An original source for V5, directly comparing validation accuracy across batch sizes and testing recipe adaptations.

source_check.notes: Resnet44 recovery combines learning-rate scaling, Ghost Batch Normalization and matched update counts; regime adaptation uses 32 times the small-batch epoch count. The authors' general explanation is an interpretation of these combined interventions.
